title: Majority Element
directAnswer: Find the element appearing more than ⌊n/2⌋ times. The intuitive answer counts frequencies in a hash map (O(n) time, O(n) space); the canonical answer is Boyer-Moore voting — keep one candidate and a counter, cancel out non-matches, and the survivor is the majority in O(n) time and O(1) space.

rules: Maintain one `candidate` and one `count` — that's the entire `O(1)` state.
When `count` hits **0**, adopt the current element as the new candidate.
Increment `count` on a match, decrement on a mismatch — each mismatch **cancels** one candidate vote.
The majority element survives because it has **more votes than everything else combined**.
No final verification needed when a majority is *guaranteed* to exist (it is, per the prompt).
Boyer-Moore finds the >n/2 element only — for >n/3 you need two candidates.
whenToUse: An element is guaranteed to appear **more than half** the time
You need `O(1)` space — can't afford a frequency map
Counting 'is there a strict majority?' over a sequence
antiSignals: Need the element appearing > n/3 (or > n/k) → extended Boyer-Moore with k−1 candidates
No guarantee a majority exists → you must add a verification pass
Need full frequency distribution → use a hash map
Array is sorted → the middle element nums[n/2] is the answer in O(1)
remember.takeaway: Boyer-Moore voting trades the hash map's O(n) space for a single counter by pairing off and cancelling opposing votes. The invariant — a true majority can never be fully cancelled because it outnumbers all others combined — is the reusable insight, and it generalises to the > n/3 and > n/k variants.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can go past the obvious hash-map count to the O(1)-space Boyer-Moore voting algorithm, and articulate WHY the cancellation invariant guarantees the survivor is the majority.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Resetting the candidate on every mismatch instead of only when count hits 0, or assuming Boyer-Moore works without a majority guarantee (it can return a wrong element if none exists).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the hash-map baseline, then derive Boyer-Moore from the 'pair off opposite votes' image. Mention the divide-and-conquer O(n log n) middle ground and the > n/3 generalisation.

problemStatement:
Given an array `nums` of size `n`, return *the majority element*.

The majority element is the element that appears **more than** `⌊n / 2⌋` times. You may assume that the majority element ***always exists*** in the array.
constraints: A majority element is guaranteed to exist
understanding: Exactly one value occupies more than half the array. Because its count strictly exceeds the count of all other values combined, it dominates any pairwise cancellation — that's the structural fact every efficient solution exploits.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is a majority element guaranteed to exist?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. That guarantee is what lets Boyer-Moore skip a verification pass — without it, the survivor would only be a candidate that still needs checking.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Strictly more than n/2, or at least n/2?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Strictly more than ⌊n/2⌋. That strictness is essential: it means the majority's votes exceed all others combined, so it can't be fully cancelled.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array contain negative or duplicate values?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes to both. We compare values for equality only, so sign and duplicates don't matter.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What space complexity do you want?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The intended answer is O(1). A hash map is O(n) space and a fine first cut, but Boyer-Moore is what the problem is really testing.

examples.explanation: 3 appears twice out of three elements — more than ⌊3/2⌋ = 1.
2 appears four times out of seven — more than ⌊7/2⌋ = 3.
A single element is trivially the majority.

approaches.name: Hash Map Frequency Count (Naive)
approaches.whenToMention: State this first — it's the obvious correct solution. Then offer to cut the O(n) space with voting.
hints: The definition is literally about counts: which value appears more than n/2 times? What structure tracks 'how many times have I seen each value'?
Walk the array, incrementing a count per value in a hash map.
Either check after each increment whether the count crossed n/2, or do a second pass over the map to find the max. Return that value.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass to build the map plus O(1) average increments → O(n) time. The map can hold up to n distinct keys → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Translate the definition directly: count how often each value appears, then return the one whose count exceeds `⌊n/2⌋`. A hash map from value to running count does exactly this in one pass; you can return early the instant a count crosses the threshold.

**Why this is the natural first attempt.** The problem is phrased in terms of frequencies — *"appears more than n/2 times"* — so the most faithful translation is to actually tally frequencies. A hash map answers *"how many of value x have I seen?"* in `O(1)` average, so the whole thing is one linear scan with a counter per key. It's impossible to get wrong, which makes it a great baseline to state out loud.

**Why the early return is safe.** Because a majority is guaranteed, the moment any value's count exceeds `n/2` you've found it — no other value can also exceed `n/2` (two values each over half would total more than `n` elements). So you can bail out as soon as a counter crosses the line, often before finishing the scan.

**Why it leaves something on the table.** It spends `O(n)` memory to remember counts you mostly don't care about — you only need *one* value at the end. Interviewers pose Majority Element specifically to see whether you can collapse that bookkeeping into a single counter. The hash map is the answer that *works*; it's not the answer that *impresses*.

**Why it still matters.** It's the correctness anchor. When you later claim Boyer-Moore returns the majority, you can sanity-check against the intuition the hash map makes obvious: the majority is simply the value with the biggest tally, and Boyer-Moore is a clever way to find that value without storing all the tallies.
approaches.insight: Counting is the literal reading of the problem, and it exposes the key fact: only one value can exceed n/2. That uniqueness is exactly what Boyer-Moore exploits to avoid storing every count.

pitfalls: Using O(n) space when the problem expects O(1) — fine as a baseline only.
Comparing with >= n/2 instead of > n/2 — the majority is strictly more than half.
Forgetting integer division semantics of n/2 (it's ⌊n/2⌋).

approaches.name: Boyer-Moore Voting (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Describe it as 'pair off each majority vote against a non-majority vote — the majority can't be fully cancelled'.
hints: You only ever need one value at the end. Could you get away with remembering just a single candidate and a counter, instead of every count?
Keep candidate and count. On each element: if count is 0, set candidate to this element. Then count++ if it matches the candidate, else count--.

Think of count as 'how many unmatched votes the current candidate has'. A mismatch cancels one vote. Because the majority has more votes than everyone else combined, it can never be cancelled to extinction — the final candidate is the answer.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single pass with O(1) work per element → O(n) time. Only two scalar variables (candidate, count) are stored → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Sweep the array maintaining a single `candidate` and an integer `count` of its currently unmatched votes. When `count` is `0`, the candidate slot is empty, so adopt the current element. Then add one vote if the element equals the candidate, or cancel one vote if it doesn't. The `candidate` left standing at the end is the majority.

**The cancellation image.** Imagine every element is a person voting for itself, and we repeatedly pair up two people who voted differently and send both home — their votes cancel. After all possible cancellations, whoever remains in the room is the survivor. Now here's the invariant: the majority element has **strictly more than n/2** votes, which is strictly more than *all other elements combined* (they total fewer than n/2). Each cancellation removes one majority vote and one non-majority vote at most, so the non-majority side runs out of votes first. The majority can never be reduced to zero, so it must be the survivor. `count` is exactly the size of the 'unpaired' group for the current candidate.

**Why we only re-anchor when `count == 0`.** `count` measures how many votes the current candidate still has after cancellations. While `count > 0`, the candidate is still 'winning' the local tug-of-war, so a mismatch just trims its lead (`count--`). Only when `count` reaches `0` is the candidate fully cancelled and the slot genuinely empty — that's the one moment it's safe to switch to a new candidate. Switching on every mismatch instead (a common bug) throws away the running tally and breaks the invariant.

**Why no verification pass is needed here.** Boyer-Moore in general only produces a *candidate* — if no true majority exists, the survivor can be an arbitrary element, so you'd normally add a second pass to count it and confirm `> n/2`. This problem *guarantees* a majority exists, and a guaranteed majority is always the survivor, so we can return `candidate` directly. (Mention the verification pass anyway — it shows you understand the algorithm's limits.)

**Why this is strictly better than the hash map.** Same `O(n)` time, but the entire memory footprint is two integers regardless of how many distinct values appear. It's also a one-pass streaming algorithm: you could run it over a data stream you can't store. That space win is the reason interviewers prize this solution.
approaches.insight: Boyer-Moore is the realisation that you don't need every count to find the most frequent value when it's a strict majority — you only need to track whether it's still 'ahead' after pairing off opponents. The invariant 'a strict majority can't be fully cancelled' is the load-bearing idea, and it extends: for > n/3 you track two candidates, for > n/k you track k−1.

Pair off opposing votes: +1 on a match, -1 on a mismatch.

pitfalls: Re-assigning candidate on every mismatch instead of only when count == 0 — breaks the invariant.
Returning candidate when no majority is guaranteed — needs a verification pass first.
Initialising count to a nonzero value, so the first element is never adopted as candidate.
Trying to extend this directly to > n/3 with one candidate — that needs two candidates.

commonMistakes: Resetting the candidate on every mismatch rather than only when count reaches 0.
Assuming Boyer-Moore is valid without a majority guarantee — it needs a verify pass otherwise.
Using a hash map (O(n) space) when the problem is asking for the O(1) voting trick.
Comparing counts with >= n/2 instead of strict > n/2.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Re-anchoring on every mismatch
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Switching candidate whenever the current element differs (rather than only when count is 0) discards the accumulated lead and can latch onto a minority element.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning the candidate with no majority guarantee
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Without a guaranteed majority, Boyer-Moore yields only a candidate. On nums = [1,2,3] it returns some element that isn't a majority. A verification pass is mandatory when existence isn't promised.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Strict vs non-strict majority threshold
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The majority must appear MORE than ⌊n/2⌋ times. Using >= can wrongly accept a value that ties at exactly half (only possible to misjudge in the hash-map verification variant).

followupVariations.title: Majority Element II
followupVariations.hint: Find all elements appearing > n/3 times — extended Boyer-Moore with two candidates and counters.

followupVariations.title: Check If a Number Is Majority Element in a Sorted Array
followupVariations.hint: Binary search the first and last occurrence; majority iff last - first + 1 > n/2.

followupVariations.title: Online Majority Element In Subarray
followupVariations.hint: Answer majority queries on subarrays — random sampling plus binary search on occurrence indices.

patternNote: Canonical Boyer-Moore majority voting. Recognise it whenever a strict majority (> n/2) is guaranteed and O(1) space matters. The cancellation invariant — a strict majority can't be fully cancelled — generalises to > n/3 (two candidates) and > n/k (k−1 candidates). Hash-map counting is the obvious O(n)-space cousin.
